title: You would have skipped her.
paragraphs: If you knew her past… you would have kept your distance.
Here’s the tension we don’t like to talk about:

We love the idea of grace…
until grace has a history.

We celebrate redemption…
until the redeemed walks into our space.

Rahab wasn’t just “a sinner.”
She was known.

Labeled.
Whispered about.
Defined by what she did in the dark.
And yet Scripture does something shocking.
“Salmon the father of Boaz by Rahab…” (Matthew 1:5)

Because God didn’t erase her past from the record—
He redeemed it into the story of Jesus.
We think redemption means hiding the past.
God says redemption means rewriting the future.

Rahab believed God when everything around her said she shouldn’t.
She hid the spies.
She turned her back on her old life.
She cast her hope on a God she barely knew yet deeply trusted.
“By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish…” (Hebrews 11:31)

Some scholars interpret this as intentional—
that Scripture keeps her past visible so grace becomes undeniable.
Now here’s where it cuts deep.

He doesn’t marry a reputation.
He receives a redeemed woman.
And in doing so, he becomes part of something eternal.
That kind of obedience costs something.
Because loving redeemed people will confront your pride.
It will expose what you really believe about grace.
It’s harder to live like, “God has fully restored them.”
We remember what God chose to forget.

We say, “Yes, they’re forgiven…”
but we whisper, “Be careful.”
And maybe this is where you are.
Carrying a past that still echoes.

Smiling in public…
but replaying your failures in private.

You’ve heard the sermons.
You’ve read the verses.
But deep down, there’s a question:
“Can God really use someone like me?”
The Gospel is not God tolerating you.
It is God transforming you through Jesus Christ.
You were not saved to sit on the sidelines of grace.
You were saved to be woven into God’s redemptive story.
And that only happens one way.
Because here is the truth we cannot soften:
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).
Jesus Christ didn’t come to improve your image.
He came to carry your sin.
To absorb the wrath we deserved.
“But God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8).
And on that cross, something holy happened.
Your identity was no longer defined by what you did—
but by what Christ has done.
“If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation…” (2 Corinthians 5:17)

So when Salmon married Rahab,
he wasn’t ignoring her past.
He was honoring God’s work in her.
That is what grace looks like when it becomes real.
A redeemer in his own right.

A woman once defined by sin
became part of the lineage of salvation.
God is not limited by your past.
He is glorified through your redemption.
So here’s the question that won’t leave you alone:
Are you still calling yourself what Jesus already paid for?
Or are you ready to believe what God says about you now?
And to the ones struggling with judgment:
Are you honoring what God has redeemed?
Or are you still holding people hostage to who they used to be?
Because the same grace you withhold from others—
is the grace you desperately needed.
And let Jesus do what only He can do.
